articles.title: The press is working. The rest-defence is not.
articles.excerpt: Eleven games into the title defence, one phase of play accounts for almost all of Arsenal's rise in expected goals against — and it is not the one everyone is arguing about.
articles.body:
Arsenal have conceded nine goals in eleven league games, a record that puts them second in the division for defensive solidity and has carried them to the top of the table. The problem is that the shots they are giving up do not look like the shots of a side top of the table.

Expected goals against has climbed from 0.91 per game at this stage last season to 1.42 this season — a fifty-six per cent increase — and almost all of that movement comes from one phase of play. Not set pieces, not the low block, but the moments immediately after Arsenal lose the ball high up the pitch.

Break the concessions down by phase and the picture sharpens. Arsenal are better than last season at defending the box, better from corners, and marginally better in open play against a settled opponent. Everything they have lost, they have lost in transition.

Nearly half a goal per game, from one phase. Over a 38-game season that is roughly eighteen expected goals of additional exposure — historically, the difference between a title and a distant second.

The full-backs are pushing five to seven metres higher than last season, and the single pivot now covers a channel two players used to share. On the whole it is a trade Arteta has made deliberately — Arsenal are creating more too. Whether it holds through a winter of midweek football is the question the next six weeks will answer.
articles.imageCaption: Mikel Arteta watches from the technical area at Villa Park. (IMAGO / Action Plus)

articles.title: The wage-structure question Chelsea must answer before January
articles.excerpt: With the squad cost ratio tightening and amortisation commitments looming, how Chelsea handle their midfield contracts will define their winter window.
articles.body:
Chelsea's financial landscape for January 2027 is dominated by one metric: the Premier League's Squad Cost Rule. While headline transfer fees have dominated the discourse, the real constraint lies in the wage bill and amortisation curves.

The club must decide whether to sanction a high-earning marquee midfield signing from Porto or lean into Cobham promotions that protect their PSR margin. Every calculation points to an amortisation cliff that requires decisive offloading before any permanent incoming deal can be registered.
articles.imageCaption: Stamford Bridge under lights ahead of a pivotal European fixture.

articles.title: De Zerbi's rebuild in five numbers: progression up, control down
articles.excerpt: Progressive passes have jumped by 14 per 90, but Spurs are facing more shots in transition. An analytical deep-dive into Tottenham's tactical identity.
articles.body:
Tottenham under Roberto De Zerbi have become the Premier League's most volatile tactical experiment. Field tilt has risen by 11%, ball progression through the central channel is up by 14 passes per 90, yet defensive box-entry prevention has dropped into the bottom quartile.

The Italian tactician is demanding aggressive rest-defence from his full-backs, asking them to act as auxiliary playmakers while leaving immense space in behind. It is football on a knife-edge — exhilarating when it clicks, catastrophic when intercepted.

articles.title: "We were told to stop playing out": a former Cobham coach on the academy's lost decade
articles.excerpt: Twelve years at the club, four academy directors, and one instruction that changed everything. An unvarnished look inside youth football's most prolific system.
articles.body: In an exclusive 90-minute sit-down, a long-serving youth coach reveals the internal philosophical tug-of-war at Cobham across four managerial regimes. From the early emphasis on physical dominance to the technical revolutions and the recent multi-club pathway pressures, this is the inside story of how modern footballers are truly made.

articles.title: The scouting network Arsenal quietly rebuilt in South America
articles.excerpt: Four appointments in eighteen months, none announced. We spoke to three of them about Arsenal's recruitment revolution in Brazil, Argentina, and Colombia.
articles.body: While competitors spent millions on algorithmic aggregation tools, Arsenal quietly established a proprietary boots-on-the-ground scouting network across South America. By embedding localized talent evaluators across youth tournaments in Sao Paulo, Buenos Aires, and Cali, the Gunners have secured early looks at tomorrow's stars before valuation spikes occur.
articles.imageCaption: South American talent spotting has become Arsenal's primary market edge.

articles.title: Inside the recruitment meeting that reshaped the Spurs shortlist
articles.excerpt: How data targets and De Zerbi's positional demands collided to eliminate four senior names and greenlight two January priorities.
articles.body: Behind closed doors at Hotspur Way, Tottenham's recruitment committee met for six hours last Thursday. On the table: the exact profiles required for De Zerbi's double-pivot and inverted full-back roles. What emerged was a ruthless pruning of previously favored targets in favor of high-press specialists.

articles.title: The single-pivot problem, explained with every touch map from the last six games
articles.excerpt: Two players used to share a channel. Now one covers it alone, and the data shows exactly where it breaks.
articles.body: By overlaying defensive actions and possession turnovers across Arsenal's last six matches, a striking trend emerges in Zone 14. When the lone defensive midfielder is drawn wide to cover an overlapping full-back, the central channel is vacated for an average of 4.2 seconds — ample time for elite Premier League counter-attacks.

articles.title: Alonso's build-up has changed three times in six weeks — here is the pattern
articles.excerpt: From a back-three diamond to asymmetric full-backs, how Chelsea's manager is attempting to bypass elite mid-blocks.
articles.body: Xabi Alonso's tactical agility has been on full display at Stamford Bridge. In August, Chelsea initiated from a structured 3-2 buildup. By mid-September, the left-back inverted into the half-space. Today, Chelsea are deploying a dynamic 2-4 base that creates overloads in wide areas with a 68% buildup success rate.

articles.title: The four Hale End teenagers who will train with the first team

articles.body: Arsenal's academy continues to deliver elite prospects. Ahead of a packed winter schedule, four Hale End standouts aged 17 and 18 have been integrated into first-team sessions at London Colney, demonstrating the technical security Arteta demands.

articles.body: Arsenal supporters can breathe a sigh of relief. William Saliba has passed medical tests and taken part in full contact training. Arteta confirmed in his pre-match briefing that the center-back will be ready for the weekend fixture.

community.title: Are we actually watching a rest-defence problem, or just variance? Eleven games is not a season
community.content: Read the xGA piece this morning and I buy most of it, but 0.47 of the jump comes from counters and we have played three of the four quickest sides in the league already. Genuine question for the people who track this properly — at what point does the sample stop being noise?

replies.content: Fair challenge, and I said as much in the piece. Phase-level xGA stabilises around fifteen to eighteen games, so we are not there. What makes me think it is signal rather than noise is that the full-back height has moved too, and that is a choice rather than a sample.
Same thing happened to us under Ange and it took a full season for anyone to call it. The full-back height is the tell every time.

community.title: The wage structure: who is actually blocking January?
community.content: Chelsea's amortisation cliff: what the 2026 accounts actually show. A breakdown of the squad cost ratio and why the January headroom is smaller than reported. Not ours and not a TPL take — but it is the clearest thing I have read on the squad cost ratio, and it lines up with Nathan's piece last week.

community.title: Three signings from a title race — which three?
community.content: De Zerbi said we are three signings away. We clearly need a press-resistant pivot, another left-sided defender who can invert, and a reliable secondary goalscorer. Who fits those profiles in January without paying £80m premiums?
